$dict.label: roth_bracket_strategy
$dict.description: NONE | FILL_CURRENT_BRACKET | FILL_TARGET_BRACKET | PARTIAL_TARGET_BRACKET | IRMAA_GUARDED | SURVIVOR_TAX_AWARE | RMD_REDUCTION | LEGACY_TARGETED | OPTIMIZER_CHOOSES | FIXED_DOLLAR | PHASE_VARYING; strategy family considered by the Roth optimizer.

$dict.label: roth_target_bracket_rate
$dict.description: 10.00% | 12.00% | 22.00% | 24.00% | 32.00% | 35.00% | 37.00%; Default target marginal bracket ceiling used by bracket-fill policies -- conversions fill up to (but not over) this bracket each year. Decision rule: in the 10-12% bracket, filling those brackets with conversions is almost always worthwhile. In 22-24%, it depends on whether future brackets (after RMDs and Social Security both start) are expected to be equal or higher -- a detailed year-by-year projection matters more than a rule of thumb here. Above 32%, converting further usually costs more today than it saves later, unless done in a low-income gap year (e.g. early retirement before Social Security or RMDs begin).

$dict.label: roth_phase_first_bracket_rate
$dict.description: 10.00% | 12.00% | 22.00% | 24.00% | 32.00% | 35.00% | 37.00%; PHASE_VARYING strategy only -- bracket rate to fill until the first Social Security claim year.

$dict.label: roth_phase_second_bracket_rate
$dict.description: 10.00% | 12.00% | 22.00% | 24.00% | 32.00% | 35.00% | 37.00%; PHASE_VARYING strategy only -- bracket rate for the next phase (second SS claim year if roth_phase_count is 3, otherwise the window end).

$dict.label: roth_phase_third_bracket_rate
$dict.description: 10.00% | 12.00% | 22.00% | 24.00% | 32.00% | 35.00% | 37.00%; PHASE_VARYING strategy only -- bracket rate for the final phase through the conversion window end. Unused when roth_phase_count is 2.

$dict.label: roth_phase_count
$dict.description: 2 | 3; PHASE_VARYING strategy only -- number of rate phases (degrades to 2 automatically for a single-member household or same-year claimants).

$dict.label: roth_fixed_annual_amount
$dict.description: Annual amount for fixed_dollar policy

$dict.label: roth_optimize_terminal_weight
$dict.description: Weight on after-tax terminal net worth in the optimizer objective. Raising this relative to the lifetime-tax weight biases the optimizer toward maximizing what's left at the end of the plan (and passed to heirs) -- it will convert more, earlier, even if that means paying more tax along the way, because Roth dollars compound tax-free for longer.

$dict.label: roth_optimize_lifetime_tax_weight
$dict.description: Weight on lifetime tax penalty in the optimizer objective. Raising this relative to the terminal-wealth weight biases the optimizer toward smoothing the household's tax bill across the whole plan -- it will convert less aggressively, trading some terminal net worth for lower total taxes paid along the way.

$dict.label: roth_optimize_terminal_pretax_tax_rate
$dict.description: Haircut on end-of-plan pre-tax balances: the tax rate the optimizer subtracts from pre-tax IRA/401(k) money still left at the end of the plan, because heirs will owe income tax on it. Left at the 24% default, it is derived per-plan as an effective SECURE Act 10-year-rule rate from the terminal balance and heir_filing_status; any other value is honored as an explicit override.

$dict.label: heir_filing_status
$dict.description: Assumed beneficiary filing status used to derive the effective SECURE Act 10-year-rule ordinary tax rate on inherited pre-tax (IRA/401k) balances in Roth optimizer scoring: Single | MFJ | HOH | MFS

$dict.label: heir_other_taxable_income
$dict.description: Assumed heir other taxable income per year (plan-start dollars, grown with the bracket inflator) that inherited pre-tax (IRA/401k) distributions stack on when deriving the effective SECURE Act 10-year-rule heir tax rate used by the Roth optimizer and after-tax estate. 0 = heir's only income; default assumes a high-earning working-age heir household ($200,000 in today's dollars). A non-default heir rate override is honored instead.

$dict.label: roth_irmaa_target_tier
$dict.description: TIER_1 | TIER_2 | TIER_3 | TIER_4 | TIER_5; IRMAA target tier threshold used when Roth conversions are capped by Medicare premium guardrails. This matters because IRMAA works on a 2-year lookback: a conversion that pushes this year's income over a tier line raises BOTH spouses' Medicare Part B and Part D premiums for a full plan year, starting two years from now -- not this year, and not just the spouse who did the conversion. Dollar thresholds come from the annual IRMAA tax table for the household's current filing status (e.g. a surviving spouse filing Single after the first death is capped at the Single-filer threshold, not the MFJ one).

$dict.label: hsa_consume_by
$dict.description: Deadline for consuming the HSA: second_death_pNN for a longevity percentile, or an explicit year. $dict.label: roth_tax_discount_rate
$dict.description: Time-value rate for comparing taxes across years: the nominal annual rate the Roth optimizer uses to convert taxes paid in different years into present-day dollars, shown as a percent such as 6.50%. Nominal because the tax and wealth figures it discounts are projected in nominal dollars; set it near your expected long-run portfolio return, not near inflation -- a rate set too low (e.g. near inflation) systematically understates Roth value, because it discounts the future tax savings more slowly than the portfolio generating them actually compounds. Rule of thumb by current federal bracket: 10-12% bracket -> 0% discount needed (Roth is almost always better); 22-24% -> 5-10% (neutral zone, model it carefully); 32%+ -> 10%+ (pre-tax is usually preferred unless converting in low-income gap years).
